newsitem.title: ISRAEL: PLO expects Netanyahu's Likud to accept state.
newsitem.headline: PLO expects Netanyahu's Likud to accept state.

text.p: The PLO's chief negotiator said on Friday he was convinced that following the Hebron deal, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party would ultimately agree to a Palestinian state.
Mahmoud Abbas, better known as Abu Mazen, spoke to Reuters within hours of Israel's completing its withdrawal from most of Hebron in the West Bank.

"We needed time to reach an understanding with the Likud government which came to power rejecting everything. That time was not wasted however because the Likud has now understood it has to live with and respect existing accords signed with its predecessor," said chief PLO negotiator Mahmoud Abbas.

Netanyahu came to power in June on a platform opposed to swap occupied Arab land for peace. But he also promised to respect Israel's international agreements, including deals -- signed by the left-centre government he ousted -- to hand over 80 percent Hebron and other parts of the West Bank.

"We are aware that we will have a battle with the Likud at every step in upcoming difficult and sensitive 'final-status' talks, and for the Likud to shift from the extreme right to the extreme left needs time," Abu Mazen said.

Netanyahu and his right-wing Likud Party reject the establishment of a Palestinian state in the West Bank and Gaza, the Palestinian goal of more than three years of negotiations with the Jewish state.

"We have the time and we are prepared because we are confident that at the end of those talks with the Likud we will end up with an independent Palestinian state with Arab East Jerusalem as its capital," Abu Mazen said.
Palestinians regard Arab East Jerusalem as their future capital. Netanyahu insists that East Jerusalem, occupied in the 1967 Middle East war and annexed, remain in Israeli hands.

The basis of future disputes emerged fewer than 48 hours after Israel and the PLO initialled the deal with Israel and the PLO interpreting differently the provision for three further withdrawals from the West Bank over the next 18 months.
PLO officials said the test of Netanyahu's commitment to the accords would be his withdrawal from rural West Bank areas.
According to Palestinians, after the three withdrawals, 90 percent of the West Bank would be under PLO rule.
Israelis say the percentage of land to be handed over to the PLO would be far less and determined by Israel alone.
Despite the Hebron pullback, little trust has developed between the PLO and Israel's Likud government.
"With this government we will continue to need international and Arab support at every step of our negotiations," said Nabil Abu Rdainah, adviser to Palestinian President Yasser Arafat.
